text:
On the third floor of St. Anselm's, the maternity rooms were arranged around a central nurses' station like spokes of a wheel, though none of the doors opened where I expected them to. All night, women in striped hospital gowns appeared in the corridor wearing the same baffled expression, as if they had stepped out for ice and returned to find the building subtly altered. One of them stood outside my room at two in the morning and asked whether this was where the babies were kept.

"I think they bring them to us," I said.

She considered this. "That doesn't sound right."

She was tall and narrow-shouldered, with a plastic bracelet on each wrist and a fine gold chain at her collar. Later I learned her name was Sylvie Vale and that she had given birth three hours after me, in the room directly across the hall. At that moment she was simply a woman holding the wall with one hand. A nurse came around the corner and steered her back toward bed.

"They wander," the nurse told me, not unkindly. "It's the epidural."

I had not had an epidural, but I didn't correct her. By then I was no longer confident about what I had or had not been given. My daughter had been born at eleven minutes past eleven, during a change of shift. For a few minutes she lay on my chest, slick and outraged, with one ear folded neatly against her head. She had a wine-colored mark on her right shoulder, just below the collarbone, shaped like the wing of a small bird.

My husband, Miles, kept touching her foot with the back of his finger.

"She has your toes," he said.

I couldn't see how that was possible. Her toes were scarcely larger than grains of rice.

They took her away to be weighed, then for a blood test, then because a pediatrician wanted to look at a murmur that turned out not to be a murmur. At midnight, a maintenance alarm began to sound in the east wing. No one called it an alarm. It was a tone, three ascending notes, gentle enough to suggest we were being alerted to an opportunity rather than a danger.

Miles was sent home shortly afterward. The private room I had been promised had become unavailable when a pipe burst above it, and I was moved to a double room on the old side of the floor, where the beds were divided by a curtain printed with faded tulips. He stood beside my bed with his coat on, looking stricken.

"I can stay in the car," he said.

"Go home."

After he left, I slept in brief, animal intervals, waking each time with the conviction that something had been placed in my arms and taken away. Once I found myself holding the television remote as if it were the baby's head.

At half past one, a nurse brought my daughter back, wrapped so tightly that only her face showed. She had the stunned expression of someone who had been told astonishing news and had not yet decided whether to believe it.

"Can I see her shoulder?" I asked.

The nurse was entering something into the computer. "Her what?"

"She had a mark on her shoulder."

"Birthmarks come and go."

"In six hours?"

"Everything about them changes fast." She lowered the baby into the bassinet. "Try to sleep while she does."

I did not sleep. Every few minutes, the hallway filled with the whisper of wheels. Once I heard a nurse say, "That one's 414," and another answer, "No, 412 is 414 now."

At four, all the babies were taken to the treatment room for hearing tests. The machine in the old ward had failed, a nurse explained, and because the pediatric floor was being painted, the tests would be done in a conference room beside the nurses' station. She placed my daughter in a bassinet with a card that read GIRL VOSS. Another nurse brought the baby from behind the tulip curtain, whose card read GIRL SEABROOK, and they wheeled them out together, two small packages in translucent boxes.

At five, I got out of bed. My legs held. I pushed my IV pole into the corridor and followed the sound of crying to the nurses' station.

Seven or eight bassinets stood in a line near the treatment room. Behind them, through a glass door, I could see a long table covered with baby hats, diapers, paper charts. Nurses moved among the infants with the concentrated tenderness of people handling evidence. Sylvie Vale stood beside the last bassinet, still in her gown and gold chain.

"Which one is yours?" I asked.

She turned slowly. "I thought you had it."

"Mine has a mark on her shoulder."

"Mine has hair."

Several of the babies had hair. They looked less like individual children than like variations on an ancient, disapproving man.

A nurse came out of the treatment room. "Mothers shouldn't be here."

"We're looking for our babies," Sylvie said.

"They'll be brought back to you."

"But which ones?"

The nurse stared at her. Sylvie did not appear to be joking. Her face was empty in a way that made me think of a room after the furniture has been removed.

"The ones that belong to you," the nurse said.

The babies came back at six. Mine was sleeping so deeply that I bent to make sure she was breathing. The card on the bassinet said GIRL VOSS. The ankle band bore my name and a string of numbers. Everything was correct. The nurse announced it as she matched our bracelets: "Mom Voss, Baby Voss."

By morning, the ward had filled with sunlight and instructions. A pediatrician said the baby was perfect. A nurse removed my IV. I signed where I was told to sign. The discharge coordinator asked whether I felt ready to go home.

"No," I said.

She laughed and checked a box.

Miles arrived at ten with the clothes we had chosen weeks earlier: a onesie printed with lemons, a hat with bear ears. Everything was absurdly small. He bent over the bassinet.

"Hi, Alice."

"Maybe not Alice."

"Maybe not," he agreed.

Across the hall, Sylvie Vale was being discharged too. She stood near the elevator in a black dress and long coat while a man in a scarf argued with a nurse about insurance. Sylvie held her baby against her chest. The baby's blanket had fallen open, exposing one shoulder.

I saw the mark before I understood that I was looking for it: wine-colored, wing-shaped, just below the collarbone.

The elevator doors opened. Sylvie stepped in. Our eyes met through the crowd of relatives and balloons. For an instant her expression changed. Not alarm, or recognition. Closer to amusement—the look of someone who has watched you discover the punch line of a joke she has known all along.

Then the doors closed.

"What?" Miles said.

"Nothing," I said.

In the car, Miles drove as if transporting a piece of antique glass. Our neighborhood seemed altered by our three days' absence. The bakery had become a smoothie place, or perhaps it had always been a smoothie place.

At home he set the car seat on the rug. We stood looking down at the baby.

"Now what?" he said.

"I think we take her out."

"Out of the seat?"

"Yes."

"Are we allowed?"

I unbuckled the straps and lifted her, then carried her to the rocking chair by the window. She began to nurse. I watched the top of her head, the soft pulse at the fontanelle. Her ear, the one that had been folded, was round and smooth.

"Did the pediatrician mention her ear?" I asked.

Miles was on the sofa, one arm over his eyes. "What about it?"

"It was folded when she was born."

"It looks fine now."

I waited until he fell asleep. Then I unwrapped the baby and laid her on a blanket in the afternoon sun. Her right shoulder was bare.

No mark. Not a faint one, not a fading one. Nothing.

I checked the left shoulder, her back, her scalp. She screamed with the concentrated fury of a creature betrayed by gravity itself. I picked her up and she turned her face into my neck.

Her hospital bracelet had come loose inside the blanket. I found it later, after she had fallen asleep on my chest. The plastic was creased where the nurse had fastened it. GIRL, it said. Then a date. Then a time. Then VALE, SYLVIE.

I read it several times. VALE. Not Voss. The letters were perfectly clear.

Down the hall, the washing machine entered its spin cycle. Miles snored softly on the sofa. The baby lay warm against me, her breath smelling faintly of iron and milk.

I waited for panic. I knew what panic was: the drop in the stomach, the metallic taste, the mind reaching for telephones and authorities. I had felt it in labor, when the baby's heartbeat vanished from the monitor for nine seconds. Panic had a shape. It had instructions.

What came instead was happiness.

It was not ordinary happiness, which rises in response to good fortune. This arrived all at once, without permission, like weather moving over water. My body loosened. My eyes filled with tears. I pressed my lips to the baby's head and felt a joy so complete that for several seconds I could not remember my own name.

I knew she was not mine. The knowledge was as plain as the plastic bracelet in my hand. Somewhere, perhaps, Sylvie Vale was holding the baby with the folded ear and the wing-shaped mark. Perhaps she was sitting in another living room, in another pool of late-day light, feeling the same impossible peace.

I should have called the hospital. That thought came to me in the language of obligation. I pictured the line of bassinets, the roll of stickers curling onto the floor. I pictured forms being amended, supervisors summoned, two mothers asked to undo what had been done.

Then the baby stirred. Her eyes opened, crossed, and fixed on mine. In that instant it seemed she recognized me—not as her mother, perhaps, but as the person who had found her.

Miles woke when the room had gone blue. He came over and knelt beside the chair.

"How are you?" he asked.

"I'm happy," I said.

The word surprised us both. He touched the baby's hand, and her fingers closed around his.

Later, I took the bracelet into the bathroom and held it under the light. VALE, SYLVIE. I imagined mailing it back. I imagined cutting it into pieces. In the end, I put it in the small lacquered box on the dresser, beside my grandmother's wedding ring and the foreign coins Miles kept for no reason.

When I returned to the living room, Miles was holding the baby by the window.

"We have to call her something," he said.

The baby turned her head at the sound of his voice. Her hair, dark as wet feathers, caught the light.

"June," I said.

"It's October."

"I know."

Miles considered this. "June Vale," he said, trying it out.

I felt the name pass through the room like a hand at my back.

"June Voss," he corrected himself.

"Yes," I said.

He carried her toward me. The baby came into my arms as if returning to a place she had briefly left. I held her against my heart, which was beating fast and evenly, like a clock in another room.

That night I woke to the sound of a newborn crying and rose to check the room. Our apartment was quiet. Through the stairwell window I could see the hospital in the distance, its upper floors lit in pale rows. Somewhere behind one of those windows, babies lay in plastic boxes while women moved from room to room, looking for what belonged to them.

Back in bed, I listened to June breathe. Every few minutes she made a small sound—half sigh, half syllable—as though testing the acoustics of her new life. I put one hand on her chest. She was warm. She was real. She was not mine.

The happiness remained. It did not feel like certainty, or absolution, or even love, though love came later and in abundance. It felt like having entered a house in the dark and discovered, by touch, that every object had been arranged for me. I would have given almost anything not to give her back.

In the morning, Miles found me awake, watching her.

"How do you feel?" he asked.

June opened her eyes. In daylight they were gray, the color of rain on stone. She looked at me with an expression of profound and temporary recognition.

"I feel," I said, "as though we brought home exactly who we were supposed to."
